idiom_name: select on the arrival channel versus a resettable time.Timer (deadline, not ticker)
implementation_notes: The classic structure collapses into one goroutine that owns a time.Timer: every arrival stops/drains and Resets the timer to the silence budget, and the expiry branch of the select is the absence alarm, so the last-seen state exists only for reporting rather than for detection. Keep the timer private to that goroutine - Go's documented Reset contract only holds when no other goroutine is receiving from the timer's channel - and select on ctx.Done() so the monitor dies with the service instead of paging during shutdown. A time.Ticker is the wrong primitive here: it fires on a schedule, while a watchman needs a deadline that each arrival pushes away.
pitfalls: Resetting a time.Timer whose channel has already fired but has not been drained is the classic Go race: follow the documented Stop-then-drain-then-Reset dance (Go 1.23+ made the unbuffered case safe, but the drain form remains the portable one).
A timer must not be Reset concurrently with a pending receive on its channel, and never from two goroutines: keep the timer in exactly one owner goroutine.
time.After allocates a new timer per call; inside a receive loop it becomes garbage pressure under load, so reuse a Timer instead.
A monitor goroutine that ignores ctx.Done() keeps alerting after shutdown and keeps the process alive in tests - and a time.Ticker is never garbage-collected until Stop().
